messages.subject: Dropping duplicate RILs
parts:
R/qtl users:
 
I have been using Karl's PDF tutorial on genetic map contruction with regard to my RILself population and, as Karl sez in the tutorial, it is indeed "fun"!
 
But I have now hit a wall due to my lack of R software command experience.
 
There are some duplicate RIL pairs in my large RIL pop, and I would like retain the one member of each pair that has the fewest missing values (dashes).  In the tutorial, one member of an indentical pair of F2 individuals is dropped with the following cmds:
cg <- comparegeno(mapthis)
hist(cg[lower.tri(cg)], breaks=seq(0, 1, len=101), xlab="No. matching genotypes")
rug(cg[lower.tri(cg)])
wh <- which(cg > 0.9, arr=TRUE)
wh <- wh[wh[,1] < wh[,2],]
wh
mapthis <- subset(mapthis, ind=-wh[,2])
 
but it is the 2nd (random) member of each listed pair that is dropped, which may or may not be the one with the fewest missing genotypes.  The pull.geno and table cmds for RIL data display only an A and B genotype matrix (no missing cells in that matrix).  Any idea on how I could alter the above cmds to (automatically, if possible) drop the "less informative" member (the one with the most total missing values) of each identical RIL pair? 
 
Also, I have been trying to make the below R cmd (used by Karl for an F2 pop in the tutorial) work with my NEAR-identical RIL pairs, wherein one or a few of the mis-matched 700+ SNP loci in such pairs are quite likely to be typing errors.  However, I lack sufficient R software expertise to make the conversion, and thus, any help on this conversion would be greatly appreciated.  
> for(i in 1:nrow(wh)) { tozero <- !is.na(g[wh[i,1],]) & !is.na(g[wh[i,2],]) & g[wh[i,1],] != g[wh[i,2],] mapthis$geno[[1]]$data[wh[i,1],tozero] <- NA }
 
- Jim

messages.author: 963b6d84a823404f
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Dropping duplicate RILs
parts:
Regarding the first question: how to identify which of each pair has the most genotype data, so that you're omitting the one with the least genotype data?

You can use ntyped() to calculate the number of genotypes for each individual.

nt <- ntyped(mapthis)

Then type the following to see the results for the individuals in the 'wh' object.

nt[wh]

Or the following, to see it in the same two-column matrix as 'wh':

matrix(nt[wh], ncol=2)

Or here's a bit of code to grab the individual in each row of 'wh' with the fewest genotypes:

todrop <- rep(NA, nrow(wh))
for(i in seq(along=todrop)) {
this.nt <- nt[ wh[i,] ]
if(this.nt[1] <= this.nt[2]) todrop[i] <- wh[i,1]
else todrop[i] <- wh[i,2]
}

But, really, if you believe these are sample duplicates and you want to keep just one of each pair, you might combine the genotype data from the two, and at any marker for which they differ, drop both.

for(ch in 1:nchr(mapthis)) {
g <- mapthis$geno[[ch]]$data
for(i in 1:nrow(wh)) {
g1 <- g[wh[i,1],]
g2 <- g[wh[i,2],]
gc <- g1
gc[!is.na(g2)] <- g2[!is.na(g2)] # values where g2 is not missing
gc[!is.na(g1) & !is.na(g2) & g1 != g2] <- NA # omit mismatches
mapthis$geno[[ch]]$data[wh[i,1],] <-
mapthis$geno[[ch]]$data[wh[i,1],] <- gc
}
}

This is similar to the second bit of code you cited, but I wasn't sure what your question was about that part.

karl
